Let’s derive the maximum loss possible. Note that the answer to this problem is

must have lost 95 times, or - 95^10 dollars. The worst that could possibly happen is that Eric
answered each prediction correctly once, then the next day he incorrectly predicted 0 rain, then
the next day 1 rain, and so forth. So, Eric must predict 10^11 showers in a year, or 3.3
showers per day. This isn’t achievable, as there are only 365 days in a year! What is
achievable? Well, with some thought, Eric is not guaranteed to make any money. If he predicts
rain 67 days (from January 28th to March 23rd), and it rains 68 days, then he loses a paltry
5^10 dollars. We could ask instead if Eric can guarantee at least as much money as he makes.
If Eric predicts rain 60% of the time (a reasonable goal) then we must pay 60\% of the rain
times - 10^10 dollars, or - 0.6 \times 5^10. Or we could simply observe that if Eric would
earn at least a million dollars, then we have guaranteed he earns at least 1,000,000 \times 10.
Therefore if Eric is guaranteed at least 1 million dollars in the end, Eric can guarantee that he
makes at least 10^10 dollars. (Notice the floor. This number can easily be 10^9 for more accurate
estimates.) It is thus important to think about who is likely to make more money in a situation
like this (why wouldn’t Eric keep his money and win every time?). As always, if you don’t see
the answer and you can’t find it, try and define the loss function (the amount you get paid for a

An optimal strategy has Eric betting 10^n (where n is the integer power of ten closest to n
= (log x)/log 10) if x > 10^(-n). If x < 10^(-n), Eric takes a guaranteed loss of 10^n (with no
compromise). E.g., assume that x = 100 and thus n = -3. So Eric “takes a guess” that it will rain on

second day, but has lost 10^(-3) = 100 dollars. Then he takes a guess at each subsequent day, each
time losing an additional 10^(-3) dollars. So now he has lost 100^2 dollars. At this point Darren
would have won, so Eric “wins” x^10 – 100^2 dollars.

Optimal strategies like this will win in any circumstance provided it is available to the players.

### Hashable, the reason why ActionScript 3.0 sucks

What would you use an algorithm to hash something?

My immediate thought would be something like a local XML API.  Compare the hash of two XML documents and do something only if they match.

In ActionScript 3.0, it turns out hash tables can't be used for anything like this.  One can't store any arbitrary data type as a value in a hash table.  In fact, "anything" may not be quite right - if it's serializable, it can be stored in a hash table.  But that's about it.

Hash tables in AS3 can only contain objects which implement the IHashable interface.  This interface requires the following as the implementation of calculateHash():

• Return a 32-bit integer
• Generated in constant time
• Generated uniquely for each object
• Idempotent (multiple calls of calculateHash() yield the same result)
• Invariant across VM restarts (cache hits)

You can think of it this way: the hash table is a set of key-value pairs, and you should hash the key uniquely for each value.  You can store arbitrary values and the key is the object.  However, you can only use these objects if they're idempotent, meaning calling calculateHash() twice will always give the same result - only the first call matters.

When you use a hash table, it's in constant time because (again, think of it as key-value pairs) it takes a constant amount of time to lookup a value with a given key.  You don't need to store any data structure for the key in the hash table, and this won't slow down lookup times.

First of all, if we knew how long it takes the clock to get a 100 counts in (one hundredth) seconds then it would be easy, but we don't know this, so we can simply assume that the next 100 counts are just the same as the previous 100 (and also the following hundred counts). In other words the difference between one ten count (one-second) and another is the same for all three hundred-thousandths of a second. That means we can simply round this off to one second, so in three hundred thousandths of a second (0.0003 seconds) the clock must 'count' 300,000 to make one second.

Divide that by the rate of ticks to get the seconds per counts, then:

$Speed = 300,000 / 300 = 10,000$

Secondly, we don't know how far one hundredth of a second is, but we know in terms of speed (see previous steps). Now to find the second in kilometres:

$\frac{10,000}{60 \cdot 60} = 0.0334 = \frac{1}{3}$

$\frac{1}{3}$ seconds for one hundredth of a second. Which means 1 second in 3 seconds, therefore 100m in 300m, or $\frac{100}{300} = 0.333$

That is, the time taken is 0.333 seconds for the 100m sprint.

To convert a decimal number to a nearest power of $10$, calculate the logarithm of that number to base $10$. Then subtract from the integer part of the logarithm that you have calculated, the integral part of $\frac1{10^3}$. cut a large number of small dots of cells, one for each slide.

However, you can only cut cells out of the tissue culture at certain points
during the growing process:

number of nutrients: nutrients for growth, oxygen for respiration, and carbon
dioxide (which the cells produce as they grow) for respiration. After 24 hours
have passed in culture, the medium is no longer able to provide the needed
nutrients.

separable solution, their metabolism no longer provides enough oxygen. The
cells begin to run out of oxygen, and they die (because they cannot divide without
oxygen).

be able to divide because they are too close to the surface of the glass.

• are not grown at too great a density so that oxygen is sufficient

If you extract only the integer part of a quantity and divide by 10, the resulting power of ten will be the same as the original quantity, except for a possible negative sign. (The method P may also be applied to any number to produce a number with an integer part and fractional part, e.g., $$\frac{68}{12}$$ can be expressed as $$6+\frac{2}{3}$$ using P.) For example, if you take 0.000016 and divide it by 10, you will get 1.6 × 10-5, which is 1.6 millionths of a centimeter. Similarly, taking 1.025 and dividing it by 10 will give you 10.25. If the decimal digits are less than 100, they are simply added to the integer part. If they are greater than 100, subtract 9 times the last digit from the integer part.

Let's recall the idea behind a carry-ripple adder. Normally, the idea is that $n$ bits are added with a "carry up" mechanism (in other words, the caries propagate to the right, and when a bit should be set to $1$ then the carry is also set to $1$). This is equivalent to having one column out of $n$ columns wired to have a "carry up" pin, and one column wired to have the negative version. Then, using a half-adder in each column, the sum of the input bits can be assembled as $2^n-2$ bits, which will then have $2^n-2$ carry inputs, and so a carry-ripple adder can add $2^n-2$ bit numbers to an overall sum of $(2^n-2)$ bit number.

So, for instance, if we are adding 4 bits, we can first use a 4 bit carry-ripple adder to get $(2^4-2)$ bit output with 4 carry outputs. Then, for every carry out, we use another 4 bit carry-ripple adder to get an output with 1 bit out and 3 carry inputs. We use $3$ of these 4 bit adders, and we get (all adders need to be placed in parallel): $$(2^4-2)\oplus (2^4-2)\oplus (2^4-2)\oplus (2^4-2)=4095\oplus 4095\oplus 4095\oplus 4095=4095.$$ This is essentially the same as @quarar's answer, but without the overcounting mentioned in @Quintec's answer.

Answer:
raw_response:
64. 

The input value "bit" is small; you can therefore extract its exponent as k = 1. In this case k is the number of base-10 digits; using e.g. Python we can find k by:

>>> bin(80)[2:].count('1')
1


Now we find the required number of soldier crabs:

>>> 10**(2**6) / 80
63.75


Multiply this by 10 to give

10**(2**6)
64


which shows why "powers of ten" are so important in computing!

The carry ripple adder method is very clever. In the paper, it is called the max-residue method. The core idea is that we can increment the carry value exactly one bit at a time. (Thus the term ripple adder.) By adding 1 to the carry after every step, we easily find the position of the carry (the "max-residue"). The carry position is at most 6 (e.g. because 2**6 + 1 is 64). In other words, we can extract the last 6 bits from the sum in one go. (We do the same trick for each position of the 64-bit carry.)

E = x E + 1 / m

Also, we have E[1/(m-1)+2] = E[1/(m-1)] + E[2]. We are assuming independence of errors. We then have

Why is this sort of problem valuable in college mathematics?

The value of this problem lies in its simplicity: you don’t have to remember tons of mathematics to be able to solve these problems. You have to know what a power of 10 is and what exponents are.

Now you don’t need to know about unit fractions or number sets because the value of all of that is “only” found in Grade 5 Math. What you need is a big multiplication table to find big powers of ten fast, and you’re in business.

Now if you look at a graph of a function, chances are you are only going to care about how big the answer is.

And a lot of the things in college mathematics where a big (integer) number is important, a power of 10 is the quickest, most direct way to get there (e.g., see this blog entry where the difficulty of polynomial long division is minimized by dividing by 10).

Much more profound, perhaps, is the fact that this skill will be important throughout your college math career.

##### Density vs. Mass

Density refers to the amount of mass in a given volume. Since mass and volume are directly related to the density, you can find the density by dividing mass by volume. Some units of density we will encounter: kg/m3, g/cm3, g/mL, and oz/mL.

Some useful density conversion factors are:

• 1 mL = 1 cm3
• 1 L = 1000 mL
• 1 cm3 = 1 mL

There are many more density conversion factors out there, including

• 1 cm3 = 1 cc
• 1 L = 1 dm3

$\text{Density}\ =\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}$

To convert from a measure of volume to a measure of volume expressed as a number of cubic feet, you must multiply by 1 ft3/L. The conversion factor will be the same because both 1 ft3 and 1 L are defined by the same volume.

Example: 40 L = 120 ft3

##### Cubic Centimeters to Cubic Feet

The conversion factor between ccm and ft3 is 1.067ft3/ccm.

Example: 500 cm3 = 547 ft3

##### What is Density?

Density is mass/volume. In its most general form, we use the following definition. When volume of a unit is in meters, density is the mass per unit volume. In general:

$\text{Density}\ =\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}$

Usually, we deal with specific density. This is the density for a particular substance where the unit of mass and volume are the same. For example, when people say “how much water is in a gas tank?” they are interested in the specific density of the water. Why? Because the volume of gas in the tank is exactly the same as the volume of water!

For example, suppose that you are writing a survey to establish how people would react to a new franchise policy. Your methodology would be to establish a scale of high or low, then assign the responses to a number e.g. 10 points for low to 1 for high. A scale of high or low to ten, even if not the numerical distance from the extremities to the actual measurement is still a numerical standard for reactions. For example, one of my mathematics professors asked for a ranking scale of high to low 0 (always), 1 (less important than high) to 10 (always).

You could, for example, assign a number of points to the reaction to the franchise policy, but you could also have established a tax rate based on the “highness” of a reaction. In that case, the “highness” of a reaction would have to be converted into a monetary value. In fact, the following is the example that our professor uses, and we’re going to use here as a serious matter. Assume that you’ve made up a tax rate based on a rating (one to ten) of “highness”. If a five is “medium”, then a 3 = 20%, 4 = 40%, and so on.

This indicates that a five is the best measurement in determining a standard.

You can actually compute this probability using other techniques, but in this problem we use Fermat’s Little Theorem. Since the hash browns aren’t specified, we’ll just assume one is centered at (x, y). So by definition

$1 = \frac{x^2+y^2}{n^2} \pmod{n}$

where $n$ is the length of the hash browns, and $x$ and $y$ are dimensions of the square. Applying Fermat’s Little Theorem to $1$ we have

$1 = \frac{(x/n)^2 + (y/n)^2}{n^2}\pmod{n}$

Factoring out the $n$ and dividing by $\frac{1}{n^2}$ we get

$n = \frac{x^2+y^2}{(x/n)^2+(y/n)^2}\pmod{n}$

Thus,

$1 = \frac{(x^2/n +y^2/n)}{n^2}\pmod{n}$

$1 = \frac{x^2/n +y^2/n}{n}\pmod{n}$

$1 = \frac{x^2}{n^2} + \frac{y^2}{n^2}\pmod{n}$

Now, applying another basic Theorem of Fermat, we have

$1 = 1 + \frac{1}{n^2}\pmod{n}$

$0 = \frac{1}{n^2} \pmod{n}$

$\frac{1}{n^2} = 1 \pmod{n}$

Multiplying both sides by $n^2$ we get

$1 = n^2 \pmod{n}$

Since $n$ and $n^2$ differ by a multiple of $n$, we can solve this to yield

$n = \pm 1$

So for some, but not all, hash browns one might hit a hash brown.

work? What is the role of a “NaN” in floating point calculations?

The distinction between arithmetic and floating point arithmetic is that
floating point arithmetic allows you to represent an approximate value of a
number in a memory location. It does not explicitly represent the original
number.

The language that you use makes all your representation explicit with the
number you are manipulating. For example, your language might represent
multiplication of 20 and -2 by being both a lossy operation as well as by
specifying the exponent of the mantissa in binary. This will be true for every
system (language) you’ll ever have to use.

Thus, if the value you try to store is equal to a particular multiple of a
characteristic of the storage format, the most intuitive answer is wrong. It is
not a valid representation of this value; you have to use an approximation, or
estimate the best near-value. When this happens, a bit of magic called “round
to nearest and if it is tied, round to even” happens and your system can
produce a number that is close enough to the original value (especially if it
had no “round to nearest” component in its definition).

How does this answer the interview question? The answer is that in the course
of your work, you will have to deal with storage for numbers in your
programming language. The best approach to it is to get some sense of what
the limitations of your representation are. One place to get some information

documentation of the operating system you are using. (For example, on Linux,

### 30. Hong Kong passport system, sciwiki

Why is the Hong Kong passport system (where every HK identity card has 2 Machine Readable Zones in addition to 1 Personalization Zone (where name and picture is stored)) necessary in the first place?

Until 2002, Hong Kong used the "local-return travelers" design to reduce the number of people queuing at immigration. This design has a large MRTZ, but most important part of the identity card is stored in the Personalization Zone, where a PIN code has to be correctly inserted.

At the 1997 Hong Kong handover, the rest of China did not passively allow a visa-free entry to Hong Kong. Instead, they required all travelers entering China to have their passport and HK identity card bound together in a "Traveler's Identity Certificate".

Also, a HK HKSAR passport (UK passport) was granted to citizens of the People's Republic of China who qualified for citizenship of the HKSAR, including their children.

By 2000, the number of travelers entering China through the HKMRTZ reduced drastically, so this design was no longer necessary.

However, HK introduced the HKSAR passport in 2002. I assume this is because at the time of the 2002 passport introduction, the number of travelers passing through the Hong Kong passport checkpoint increased again, and thus the biometric identifiers of HK residents are necessary.

A heuristic way of converting a number (as a string) to the nearest power of 10 is:

• Calculate the logarithm base 10 of the number, rounded to the nearest integer,
• convert the resulting integer back to a power of 10.

As the number $$x$$ approaches zero, the result is no longer accurate, and that is acceptable, as we could end up with 0.0001, for example.

A mathematical proof of this formula will take some work to prove, and I do not know one. As the value of $$x$$ approaches zero, the decimal part $$x - \lfloor{x}\rfloor$$ becomes smaller, but the decimal part is always greater than 0, so we never drop to the $$\lfloor{x}\rfloor$$ part, which would produce the desired result. So the formula is basically just a measure of how close $$x$$ is to the nearest integer. If $$x$$ is an exact integer, we can use that as a terminal condition to prevent calculating further.

For those without a calculator handy, the results of this formula are:

$$\lfloor \log_{10}{x} \rfloor \approx \lceil \log_{10}{10^{\frac{x}{10}}}\rceil$$

Note that 9 is the first value greater than $$0.3$$ where $$\lfloor \log_{10}{x} \rfloor > \lceil \log_{10}{10^{\frac{x}{10}}}\rceil$$

# Scala Golf #6 - Min Stack

A stack is an ordered container. Items are inserted and removed only from the top. Here’s what that looks like in Scala: stack = [ ] stack.push( 1 ) stack.push( 2 ) stack.push( 3 ) stack.pop() stack.pop() println(stack) // [ 2 ] stack.push( 4 ) stack.push( 5 ) println(stack) // [ 4, 5, 2 ] 

But what if we also wanted to store and access the values in the stack? That would turn our basic stack into a Min Stack.

A Min Stack is a stack that stores not only the elements popped from the stack, but also the minimum element on the stack at each step of the operation. We provide a min() function that returns the minimum value on the stack. Note that our syntax here is stack-min = min(), while the stack is [ 5 , 3 , 4 , 2 ].

Java users might be familiar with the concept of a max stack – a stack that remembers the largest value on the stack at each step. Our concept is similar. However, we’ll store values, so we can do more useful things with our stack. Note that a max stack would be inconsistent – the max stack would be a different value than the maximum value on the stack, since the latter is determined at each step while the former is not. So to avoid confusion, let’s just go with min instead.

We’ll include a popMin() function for removing the minimum element as well. You can decide if pop() should also remove the minimum element, if you want the same pop methods to work for both cases. Our syntax for popping a minimum is stack-pop-min = popMin().

import math

def powers_of_ten(x):
    total_value = x
    expon = 0
    while True:
        try:

Using $k=6$ to find the nearest power of 10 to $\dfrac{69,000,000,000}{4}$, or $69,000,000,000 \cdot \dfrac{1}{4}$, we get

$\qquad\qquad\qquad 17,250,000,000 < 1,725,000,000 \leq 17,250,000,000$

we’d get $O(n)$. For the worst case, the average complexity would be more like the worst case complexity, ie,

The function should return the reduced fraction (as a list of two integers). If the fraction is not reduced, the function should return the “impossible” string.

Output: [1, 3]

def simplify(num, den):
den = int(den)

num_copied = num[:]
den_copied = den[:]
while den_copied != 1 and num_copied != 0:
if num_copied >= den_copied:
num_copied = num_copied // den_copied
den_copied = den_copied // 1
else:
num_copied = num_copied // 1
den_copied = den_copied // den_copied

if num_copied != 0:
return num_copied, den_copied
else:
return "impossible"

It basically takes the "big" things in a sequence, and if your equation can be broken down into a sum of such things, can give you an estimate for the rest of the sum based on the convergence of the big things. It does this using the fact that since each big thing is converging and is the sum of a sequence of smaller and smaller terms, the sum of the big terms must also converge.

The terminology was invented by the great mathematician Paul Erdős, and not surprisingly has Erdős in it. The website you linked to lists the various different sorts of similar series that can be analyzed using asymptotic techniques. The idea being that if we can break down a sequence that isn't uniformly convergent into terms that are, then an estimate for the big terms lets us know about the other terms

### 1.6 Why were four types of algorithms developed?

The main reason why different types of algorithms were developed is to efficiently solve a class of problems that has three distinct characteristics.

First, a class of problems needs to be identifiable in order to determine what methods are most appropriate. For example, the series of pizza cuts above illustrates how NP-complete problems are defined: A problem is NP-complete if there is at least one other problem whose solution is known to be at least as difficult as to solve the given one. This fact also shows that there are problems that, on the one hand, have no direct solution (e.g., ordering five items when we want at least two of them to be identical), and, on the other hand, can be used to characterize other problem (e.g., deciding whether an input string is a palindrome). The above pizza-cutting algorithm can be transformed into a graph-cutting algorithm for graph connectivity. Similarly, the VLSI problem of finding shortest paths in graphs of “handedness”, using maximum bandwidth between all source nodes and all sink nodes, has been treated by numerous graph-cut algorithms.

The second characteristic is that some problems can be solved in polynomial time on some input sizes, but not on the entire range of input sizes. For example, finding the number of jobs that have been scheduled by a precedence graph processor (see Section 1.7 in this Chapter) is in P, but finding out which sets of jobs are compatible is NP-complete. The latter problem is not polynomial on all the input instances, but it does have a polynomial-time solution for some of them. Maximum bandwidth path problems and traveling salesman problems are good examples of polynomial-time hard problems that are computed in polynomial time for some, but not all, instances.

Solution: Step 1: Prove
The number of Dyck paths ending in the origin $(0,0)$ is
$${{8n} \choose {n}}$$.
Step 2: Derive the formula
The number of Dyck paths from $(0, 0)$ to $(m, m)$ can be obtained by placing $m$ perfect squares
in an $8 \times 8$ grid. Each of those $m$ squares is filled with $2$ unit blocks. In addition, you can place $2$ unit blocks in
two of the $16$ corners ($2$ possibilities for the first corner, $2$ for the second corner, $2$ for the third corner, and so on).
We are finally left with $8 \times 8 - 16 = 56$ unit blocks and by the same argument that for any $m$, the number of Dyck
paths from $(0, 0)$ to $(m, m)$ is
$$\sum_{k=0}^m {{8k} \choose {k}}$$
Or equivalently, the number of Dyck paths from $(0, 0)$ to $(m, m)$ is
$$\sum_{k=0}^m {{8k} \choose {k}} = \sum_{k=0}^m {2k \choose k} 2^k$$
Since we need a second route from the origin $(0, 0)$ to $(m, m)$, where the path is restricted to the
horizontal axis with no blocks (only $2$ unit blocks can be used, and that too is restricted only to the same
the diagonal), the required number of paths is
$$\frac{2}{2}\left( \sum_{k=0}^m {{8k} \choose {k}} \right) = {{8n} \choose {n}}$$
Note that there are $n$ routes from the origin to $(n,n)$ (one on each row of a rectangular grid starting from $n$ blocks)
and in each route $n$ blocks are used. Therefore, for any $n$,
the total number of Dyck paths from $(0, 0)$ to $(m, m)$ is
$$\sum_{k=0}^m {{8n} \choose {n}}$$

It is produced by many different kinds of objects, each with different methods of excitation and emission, and each creating its own continuum. For instance, continuum radiation by conventional incandescent light bulbs has a black body distribution which can be experimentally or theoretically described by the Planck distribution.
